if (requireNamespace("kableExtra", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    to <- tryCatch(knitr::pandoc_to(), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(to)) to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
    if (!is.null(to) && to == "docx") {
      kable_styling_orig <- get("kable_styling", envir = asNamespace("kableExtra"))
      assignInNamespace("kable_styling", function(kbl, ...) {
        args <- list(...)
        args$bootstrap_options <- NULL
        do.call(kable_styling_orig, c(list(kbl), args))
      }, ns = "kableExtra")
    }
  }, error = function(e) invisible(NULL))
}

# Cousineau-Morey within-subject SE helper
# Args:
#   df          - data frame (one row per subject × cell)
#   value_col   - bare column name of the measurement (e.g. accuracy, rt)
#   subject_col - bare column name of subject ID
#   ...         - grouping variables for the summary (e.g. task, difficulty, effort)
# Returns a grouped tibble with columns: ..., mean_val, n, cm_se
calc_within_se <- function(df, value_col, subject_col, ...) {
  grp_vars   <- rlang::ensyms(...)
  val_sym    <- rlang::ensym(value_col)
  subj_sym   <- rlang::ensym(subject_col)

  grand_mean <- mean(df[[rlang::as_string(val_sym)]], na.rm = TRUE)

  df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!subj_sym) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(.subj_mean = mean(!!val_sym, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(.norm = !!val_sym - .subj_mean + grand_mean) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!!grp_vars) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_val = mean(!!val_sym, na.rm = TRUE),
      n        = dplyr::n(),
      .cm_se_raw = sd(.norm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
      M        = dplyr::n_distinct(interaction(!!!grp_vars)),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      # Morey (2008) correction factor: sqrt(M / (M-1))
      cm_se = .cm_se_raw * sqrt(n / (n - 1)),
      cm_ci95 = 1.96 * cm_se
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-.cm_se_raw, -M)
}

# Helper function to escape LaTeX special characters in captions
latex_escape <- function(text) {
  text <- gsub("\\\\", "\\\\textbackslash{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("([#$%&_{}])", "\\\\\\1", text)
  text <- gsub("~", "\\\\textasciitilde{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("\\^", "\\\\textasciicircum{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("$\approx$", "$\\\\approx$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("×", "$\\\\times$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("Δ", "$\\\\Delta$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("–", "--", text, fixed = TRUE)  # en dash
  text <- gsub("—", "---", text, fixed = TRUE)  # em dash
  text <- gsub("'", "`", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left single quote
  text <- gsub("'", "'", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right single quote
  text <- gsub('"', "``", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left double quote
  text <- gsub('"', "''", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right double quote
  return(text)
}

# Helper: figure path resolution
# Returns PNG for HTML output, PDF for DOCX output
fig_path <- function(fig_name) {
  # Get base name without extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(fig_name)
  
  # Detect output format - try multiple methods
  output_format <- NULL
  
  # Method 1: Check if we're rendering to LaTeX/PDF (most important for path resolution)
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    output_format <- "latex"
  }
  
  # Method 2: Check knitr's pandoc output format (most reliable)
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
    if (!is.null(pandoc_to)) {
      output_format <- pandoc_to
    }
  }
  
  # Method 3: Check if we're in a DOCX rendering context
  # Quarto sets this in the knitr options
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    # Check for DOCX-specific indicators
    docx_indicators <- c(
      knitr::opts_knit$get("quarto.document.format") == "docx",
      grepl("docx", knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format") %||% "", ignore.case = TRUE)
    )
    if (any(docx_indicators, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      output_format <- "docx"
    }
  }
  
  png_name <- paste0(base_name, ".png")
  pdf_name <- paste0(base_name, ".pdf")
  jpg_name <- paste0(base_name, ".jpg")
  
  # Find the actual file location
  png_abs <- NULL
  pdf_abs <- NULL
  jpg_abs <- NULL
  
  candidates_png <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", png_name)
  )
  
  candidates_pdf <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name)
  )
  
  candidates_jpg <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name)
  )
  
  for (path in candidates_png) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      png_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_pdf) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      pdf_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_jpg) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      jpg_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  # Choose format based on output type
  # For LaTeX: paths need to work for both R execution (with root.dir) and LaTeX compilation
  # Solution: return paths relative to root.dir for R validation, but use a wrapper in include_graphics
  # that handles LaTeX path conversion
  is_latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()
  
  if (exists("use_relative_paths") && use_relative_paths) {
    if (is_latex) {
      # LaTeX: return paths relative to reports/ directory (where LaTeX runs)
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", png_name))
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name))
      }
    } else {
      # HTML/DOCX: Return relative paths from root.dir (which is set to project root)
      if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
        if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        }
      } else {
        # HTML: prefer PNG
        if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        } else if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    # Return absolute paths when root.dir is not set
    if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    } else {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Fallback: return relative path even if file doesn't exist (let LaTeX/Quarto handle error)
  warning("Figure not found: ", fig_name, " (checked: ", paste(c(candidates_pdf, candidates_png), collapse = ", "), ")")
  if (is_latex) {
    return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
  } else {
    return(file.path("output/figures", if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) pdf_name else png_name))
  }
}

# Wrapper for include_graphics that handles LaTeX path issues
include_graphics_safe <- function(fig_path_result) {
  # For LaTeX with root.dir set, fig_path() returns "../output/figures/..." 
  # which works for LaTeX but knitr::include_graphics() validates relative to root.dir
  # Use error=FALSE to skip validation since we know the file exists (we checked in fig_path)
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_path_result, error = FALSE)
}

# Helper: safe read
sread <- function(path) {
  # Ensure path is a single character string
  if (length(path) > 1) {
    path <- path[1]  # Take first if multiple
  }
  if (length(path) == 1 && is.character(path) && file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch(read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
}

# Posterior P/CrI formatting — avoid rounding high probabilities to "1.00"
.fmt_cri <- function(lo, hi, digits = 2L) {
  if (is.na(lo) || is.na(hi)) return("")
  if (digits == 2L && max(abs(c(lo, hi))) < 0.15 && (hi - lo) < 0.08) digits <- 3L
  fmt <- paste0("%.", digits, "f")
  sprintf("95%% CrI $[%s,\\; %s]$", sprintf(fmt, lo), sprintf(fmt, hi))
}

.fmt_posterior_p <- function(p, dir = c("lt", "gt")) {
  if (is.na(p)) return("")
  sym <- if (dir[1] == "lt") "<" else ">"
  if (p >= 0.999) return(sprintf("; $P(\\beta %s 0) > .999$", sym))
  if (p <= 0.001) return(sprintf("; $P(\\beta %s 0) < .001$", sym))
  sprintf("; $P(\\beta %s 0) = %.3f$", sym, p)
}

.lmm_term <- function(tbl, pattern) {
  if (is.null(tbl) || nrow(tbl) == 0) return(NULL)
  row <- tbl %>%
    dplyr::filter(.data$effect == "fixed", grepl(pattern, .data$term, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
    dplyr::slice(1)
  if (nrow(row) == 0) return(NULL)
  list(
    beta = row$estimate,
    lo   = row$conf.low,
    hi   = row$conf.high
  )
}

pupil_data <- NULL
for (path in pupil_data_paths) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      pupil_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("sub" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(subject_id = as.character(sub))
      }
      if ("effort" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            effort == "High" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            effort == "Low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(effort)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty level from stimulus_intensity and isOddball
      if ("stimulus_intensity" %in% names(pupil_data) && "isOddball" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            isOddball == 0 | is.na(isOddball) | stimulus_intensity == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # Based on mapping: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 3=Easy, 1-2=Hard
            stimulus_intensity == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity == 3 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      # Map cognitive_auc column name (using cog_auc_w3 for Chapter 3 primary analysis)
      if ("cog_auc_w3" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        # Chapter 3 maps the Decision-Response AUC window (cog_auc_w3) as the primary TEPR predictor
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc_w3)
      } else if ("cog_auc" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc)
      }
      # Map baseline_B0 column name
      if ("baseline_B0_mean" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"baseline_B0" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(baseline_B0 = baseline_B0_mean)
      }
      # Data loaded successfully (diagnostic messages suppressed for rendering)
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      # Error loading from this path, try next (messages suppressed for rendering)
      NULL
    })
  }
}

  file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "../bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
  "data/analysis_ready/bap_ddm_only_ready.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL_full.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/behavioral_data.csv"
)

behavioral_data <- NULL
for (path in behavioral_data_paths) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      behavioral_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("subject_id" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
      }
      if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(task = case_when(
            task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
          ))
      }
      if ("same_diff_resp_secs" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = same_diff_resp_secs)
      } else if ("resp1RT" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = resp1RT)
      }
      if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(iscorr = as.integer(resp_is_correct))
      }
      # Map effort_condition from grip_level
      if ("grip_level" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty_level from stim_offset and stim_is_diff
      # Standard: stim_is_diff = FALSE or stim_offset = 0
      # Hard: Small offsets that are hard to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 8 Hz and 16 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.06 and 0.12 contrast
      # Easy: Large offsets that are easy to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 32 Hz and 64 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.24 and 0.48 contrast
      if ("stim_offset" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Ensure task column exists for mapping
        if (!"task" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
            mutate(task = case_when(
              task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
              task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
              TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
            ))
        }
        
        # Create task_type helper column for mapping
        if ("task" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- NA_character_
        }
        
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            # Standard trials
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # ADT Easy: 32 or 64 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
            # ADT Hard: 8 or 16 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
            # VDT Easy: 0.24 or 0.48 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
            # VDT Hard: 0.06 or 0.12 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
            # Fallback: infer from magnitude if stim_is_diff is TRUE
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset >= 30 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset < 30 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset >= 0.2 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset < 0.2 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            # Default to Standard
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          )) %>%
          select(-task_type)  # Remove temporary column
      } else if ("stim_level_index" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Fallback: use stim_level_index if stim_offset not available
        # NOTE: Please confirm this mapping - typically: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 2=Hard
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | stim_level_index == 0 ~ "Standard",
            stim_level_index == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stim_level_index %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            stim_level_index == 3 ~ "Easy",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      
      # Check if difficulty_level already exists but Easy trials are missing
      # If so, try to load from raw data file to get Easy trials
      if ("difficulty_level" %in% names(behavioral_data) && 
          !any(behavioral_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
        # Try to load raw data file to get Easy trials
        raw_data_paths <- c(
          file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          file.path(proj_root, "../bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"
        )
        for (raw_path in raw_data_paths) {
          if (file.exists(raw_path)) {
            tryCatch({
              raw_data <- read_csv(raw_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
              # Check if raw data has Easy trials
              if ("stim_offset" %in% names(raw_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                # Map difficulty for raw data
                if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                    mutate(task = case_when(
                      task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                      task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                      TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                    ))
                }
                if ("task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else {
                  raw_data$task_type <- NA_character_
                }
                raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                  mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
                    stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
                    TRUE ~ "Standard"
                  )) %>%
                  select(-task_type)
                
                # If raw data has Easy trials, combine with processed data
                if (any(raw_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
                  # Standardize column names to match behavioral_data
                  if ("subject_id" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
                  }
                  if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data) && !"task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(task = case_when(
                        task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                        task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                      ))
                  }
                  if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(accuracy = as.numeric(resp_is_correct))
                  }
                  if ("grip_level" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
                        grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
                        grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
                      ))
                  }
                  
                  # Combine: keep all rows from processed data, add Easy trials from raw data
                  behavioral_data <- bind_rows(
                    behavioral_data,
                    raw_data %>% filter(difficulty_level == "Easy")
                  )
                  break
                }
              }
            }, error = function(e) {
              # Silently continue if raw data can't be loaded
            })
          }
        }
      }
      
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("Error loading", path, ":", e$message, "\n")
      NULL
    })
  }
}

# Compute manipulation checks inline from behavioral_data when available (ensures fresh data on re-render)
if (!is.null(behavioral_data) && nrow(behavioral_data) > 0 &&
    requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("broom.mixed", quietly = TRUE)) {
  need_manip <- c("subject_id", "difficulty_level", "effort_condition")
  has_decision <- any(c("decision", "iscorr", "accuracy", "resp_is_correct") %in% names(behavioral_data))
  has_rt <- any(c("rt", "same_diff_resp_secs", "resp1RT") %in% names(behavioral_data))
  if (all(need_manip %in% names(behavioral_data)) && has_decision && has_rt) {
    dd_manip <- behavioral_data %>%
      mutate(
        decision = as.integer(if ("decision" %in% names(.)) decision else if ("iscorr" %in% names(.)) iscorr else if ("accuracy" %in% names(.)) accuracy else resp_is_correct),
        rt = as.numeric(if ("rt" %in% names(.)) rt else if ("same_diff_resp_secs" %in% names(.)) same_diff_resp_secs else resp1RT)
      ) %>%
      filter(difficulty_level %in% c("Easy", "Hard"), !is.na(decision), !is.na(rt), rt > 0)
    ulev <- unique(as.character(dd_manip$effort_condition))
    eff_ref <- ulev[grepl("Low|5", ulev, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
    eff_oth <- ulev[grepl("High|40", ulev, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
    if (is.na(eff_ref)) eff_ref <- ulev[1]
    if (is.na(eff_oth)) eff_oth <- ulev[ulev != eff_ref][1]
    dd_manip$effort_condition <- factor(dd_manip$effort_condition, levels = c(eff_ref, eff_oth))
    dd_manip$difficulty_level <- factor(dd_manip$difficulty_level, levels = c("Easy", "Hard"))
    dd_manip$subject_id <- factor(as.character(dd_manip$subject_id))
    if (nrow(dd_manip) > 100) {
      tryCatch({
        acc_fit <- lme4::glmer(decision ~ difficulty_level + effort_condition + (1 | subject_id),
          data = dd_manip, family = binomial())
        acc_glmm <- broom.mixed::tidy(acc_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "Wald")
        rt_med <- dd_manip %>% group_by(subject_id, difficulty_level, effort_condition) %>%
          summarise(rt_med = median(rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
        rt_fit <- lme4::lmer(rt_med ~ difficulty_level + effort_condition + (1 | subject_id), data = rt_med)
        rt_lmm <- broom.mixed::tidy(rt_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "Wald")
      }, error = function(e) NULL)
    }
  }
}

run_dir <- params$run_dir
tables_dir_abstract <- file.path(proj_root, run_dir, "tables")
PRIMARY_THR <- 0.20
PRIMARY_RT <- "probe_onset_locked"
PRIMARY_MODEL <- "additive"

fixef_link_abstract <- NULL
fixef_candidates <- c("fixef_link_scale.csv", "table_fixed_effects.csv", "primary_model_fixef.csv",
                      "primary_fixef_link_scale.csv", "ddm_fixed_effects_link_scale.csv")
for (fname in fixef_candidates) {

  if (file.exists(fpath)) {

    if (!is.null(fixef_link_abstract) && nrow(fixef_link_abstract) > 0) break
  }
}
if (is.null(fixef_link_abstract) || nrow(fixef_link_abstract) == 0) {
  if (exists("fx_table") && !is.null(fx_table) && nrow(fx_table) > 0) {
    fixef_link_abstract <- fx_table
  } else {

h1_beta_str <- "[see @tbl-hyp-summary]"
h1_cri_str  <- ""
h1_p0_str   <- ""
h1_p_in_rope_pct <- "—"
h2_beta_str <- "[see @tbl-hyp-summary]"
h2_cri_str  <- ""
h2_p0_str   <- ""
h4_beta_str <- "[see tbl-hyp-summary]"
h4_cri_str  <- ""
h4_p0_str   <- ""

if (!is.null(fixef_link_abstract) && nrow(fixef_link_abstract) > 0) {
  fl <- fixef_link_abstract
  if (!"threshold" %in% names(fl)) fl <- dplyr::mutate(fl, threshold = PRIMARY_THR)
  if (!"model" %in% names(fl)) fl <- dplyr::mutate(fl, model = PRIMARY_MODEL)
  if (!"rt_type" %in% names(fl)) fl <- dplyr::mutate(fl, rt_type = PRIMARY_RT)

  h1_row <- fl |>
    dplyr::filter(
      grepl(PRIMARY_MODEL, model, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl(PRIMARY_RT, rt_type, ignore.case = TRUE),
      threshold == PRIMARY_THR,
      !grepl("^bs_|^bias_|^ndt_", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl("effortcondition|effort.*high|high.*effort", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      !grepl("Intercept|task|difficulty", term, ignore.case = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::slice(1)

  if (nrow(h1_row) == 1) {
    h1_est <- h1_row$Estimate
    h1_lo  <- h1_row$Q2.5
    h1_hi  <- h1_row$Q97.5
    h1_se  <- if ("Est.Error" %in% names(h1_row)) h1_row$Est.Error else NA_real_

    h1_beta_str  <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.2f$", h1_est)
    h1_cri_str   <- .fmt_cri(h1_lo, h1_hi, 2L)
    h1_p0_val    <- if (!is.na(h1_se) && h1_se > 0) pnorm(0, mean = h1_est, sd = h1_se) else NA_real_
    h1_p0_str    <- .fmt_posterior_p(h1_p0_val, "lt")
    h1_se_rope   <- if (is.finite(h1_lo) && is.finite(h1_hi)) (h1_hi - h1_lo) / (2 * 1.96) else NA_real_
    if (is.finite(h1_se_rope) && h1_se_rope > 0) {
      h1_p_in_rope_pct <- sprintf(
        "%.0f%%",
        100 * integrate(function(x) stats::dnorm(x, h1_est, h1_se_rope), -0.02, 0.02)$value
      )
    }
  }

  h2_row <- fl |>
    dplyr::filter(
      grepl(PRIMARY_MODEL, model, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl(PRIMARY_RT, rt_type, ignore.case = TRUE),
      threshold == PRIMARY_THR,
      grepl("^bs_", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl("effortcondition|effort.*high|high.*effort", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      !grepl("Intercept|task|difficulty", term, ignore.case = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::slice(1)

  if (nrow(h2_row) == 1) {
    h2_est <- h2_row$Estimate
    h2_lo  <- h2_row$Q2.5
    h2_hi  <- h2_row$Q97.5
    h2_se  <- if ("Est.Error" %in% names(h2_row)) h2_row$Est.Error else NA_real_
    h2_beta_str <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.2f$", h2_est)
    h2_cri_str  <- .fmt_cri(h2_lo, h2_hi, 3L)
    h2_p0_val   <- if (!is.na(h2_se) && h2_se > 0) 1 - pnorm(0, mean = h2_est, sd = h2_se) else NA_real_
    h2_p0_str   <- .fmt_posterior_p(h2_p0_val, "gt")
  }

  h4_row <- fl |>
    dplyr::filter(
      grepl(PRIMARY_MODEL, model, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl(PRIMARY_RT, rt_type, ignore.case = TRUE),
      threshold == PRIMARY_THR,
      grepl("^bias_", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      grepl("effortcondition|effort.*high|high.*effort", term, ignore.case = TRUE),
      !grepl("Intercept|task|difficulty", term, ignore.case = TRUE)
    ) |>
    dplyr::slice(1)

  if (nrow(h4_row) == 1) {
    h4_est <- h4_row$Estimate
    h4_lo  <- h4_row$Q2.5
    h4_hi  <- h4_row$Q97.5
    h4_se  <- if ("Est.Error" %in% names(h4_row)) h4_row$Est.Error else NA_real_
    h4_beta_str <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.3f$", h4_est)
    h4_cri_str  <- sprintf("95%% CrI $[%.3f,\\; %.3f]$", h4_lo, h4_hi)
    h4_p_lt0_val <- if (!is.na(h4_se) && h4_se > 0) pnorm(0, mean = h4_est, sd = h4_se) else NA_real_
    h4_p0_val    <- if (!is.na(h4_p_lt0_val)) 1 - h4_p_lt0_val else NA_real_
    h4_p0_str    <- .fmt_posterior_p(h4_p0_val, "gt")
  }
}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Sixty-seven older adults completed auditory and visual same–different judgments under low (5% MVC) or high (40% MVC) isometric grip while pupil diameter was recorded. A hierarchical Wiener DDM was fit with probe-onset-locked RT. Difficulty entered drift ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$); task and effort entered starting-point bias ($z$), held constant across difficulty because trials were randomized.

High effort lowered drift relative to low (`r h1_beta_str`, `r h1_cri_str``r h1_p0_str`; `r h1_p_in_rope_pct` ROPE mass). High effort produced a directionally positive boundary-separation contrast that was practically negligible under the project ROPE (`r h2_beta_str`, `r h2_cri_str``r h2_p0_str`). Effort did not credibly change bias (`r h4_beta_str`, `r h4_cri_str``r h4_p0_str`). Non-decision time ($t_0$) was group-level only in the primary model, so effort on peripheral timing was not tested there; an exploratory log-$t_0$ effort term was small and wide ($\hat{\beta} = 0.02$, 95% CrI [−0.05, 0.09]).

Exploratory pupil-linked models showed near-zero TEPR associations with drift and bias, no predictive gain over the behavioral baseline on the pupil subset, and no LOO advantage for Cavanagh-style pupil→boundary extensions (@sec-pupil-ddm-integration). A pupil × difficulty interaction on drift did not support demand-dependent arousal effects (@sec-pupil-ddm-integration).

Primary contrasts held under alternative RT cutoffs and when task modality was included as a sensitivity check. Under concurrent grip, older adults mainly accumulated less evidence per unit time; caution and pre-response bias changed little.

\newpage

# Introduction

## Physical Effort and Performance in the Aging Brain

Older adults show pervasive response time slowing across virtually all task domains, a finding historically attributed to generalized processing speed decline [@birren1965age; @salthouse1985speed; @salthouse1996]. Beyond simple biological slowing, this behavior is often strategic; older adults systematically favor accuracy over speed, adopting a more cautious response mode to compensate for declining neural efficiency [@rabbitt1979old; @ratcliff2004aging; @starns2010]. While these patterns are well-documented in sedentary laboratory settings, real-world cognitive tasks frequently occur while simultaneously exerting physical effort.

For older adults, the "cost" of such exertion is significantly higher due to age-related declines in motor efficiency and reduced neural reserves [@verhaeghen2003]. According to resource competition theories, the executive demands required to maintain a physical grip or posture compete for the same limited pool of cognitive resources needed for decision-making [@wickens2008]. While it is established that physical load can impair general performance [@verhaeghen2003; @woollacott2002], we do not yet know whether this interference simply slows down peripheral execution or fundamentally degrades the quality of information processing. This study utilizes a computational framework to decompose these effects, investigating how physical effort and physiological state interact to shape decision-making in the aging brain.

## Decomposing Decisions: The Drift-Diffusion Model

To understand the latent mechanisms underlying age-related slowing, we utilize the Drift-Diffusion Model [@ratcliff1978theory]. This computational framework assumes that decision-making is a continuous process of evidence accumulation over time, driven by two primary opposing forces that define the internal dynamics of the choice. The first of these internal forces is the deterministic mean drift rate ($v$), which represents the true quality or strength of the sensory evidence extracted from a stimulus. The second force is the stochastic diffusion constant ($\sigma$), capturing the inherent noise and moment-to-moment Gaussian fluctuations in the nervous system. Together, these two forces determine the trajectory of a decision vector over time until it intersects a boundary, a dynamic process visually formalized in @fig-ddm-process (Panel B). As shown in this architectural layout, the final choice and its corresponding timing are ultimately governed by the decision architecture, which dictates the structural boundaries and thresholds within which this continuous evidence accumulation occurs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ddm-process
#| fig-cap: !expr fig1_cap
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "100%"
include_graphics_safe(main_fig("fig1_design_schematic.png"))
```

This mathematical framework allows us to decompose standard behavioral reaction time data and accuracy rates into four distinct latent parameters. The drift rate ($v$) reflects the efficiency and quality of the accumulation process itself, where the absolute magnitude of the parameter reflects the clarity of the sensory signal and the efficiency of the accumulation process itself, directing the decision vector toward either the upper ('different') or lower ('same') boundary based on stimulus properties. The boundary separation ($a$) establishes the total amount of evidence required before a participant commits to a response, serving as a direct measure of response caution. The starting-point bias ($z$) accounts for any a priori preference or baseline asymmetry toward one response alternative over another before the trial even begins. Finally, the non-decision time ($t_0$) captures the duration of peripheral mechanisms that fall completely outside the core decision process, such as initial sensory encoding and downstream motor execution [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion; @voss2004interpreting].

Decomposing these metrics is critical when examining an aging population because standard behavioral observations often mask the true underlying cognitive changes. Previous research demonstrates a clear processing dissociation in older adults. When performing simple perceptual tasks like brightness or letter discrimination, older adults consistently exhibit elevated boundary separation and longer non-decision times, yet their underlying drift rate remains remarkably preserved [@ratcliff2001aging; @ratcliff2004aging; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. However, this preservation is fragile. When task demands intensify through increased perceptual load, complex visual search, or episodic memory retrieval, the efficiency of evidence accumulation begins to decline significantly [@madden1991; @spaniol2006].

An open question is whether these DDM parameters represent rigid capacity limits or if they are dynamically modulated by an individual's immediate physiological state. By using physical effort to manipulate systemic arousal, we can test whether these internal mechanisms are flexible under stress. Specifically, we can determine if the increased physiological cost of high physical effort forces an alteration in the decision architecture, perhaps prompting a compensatory increase in boundary caution, or if it directly degrades the efficiency of the evidence accumulation process itself. This methodology allows us to move past the simple observation that older adults slow down under pressure, revealing instead the real-time interaction between somatic demand and cognitive efficiency.

## Arousal, Effort, and Decision Performance in Older Adults

The relationship between physiological arousal and cognitive performance has long been conceptualized as an inverted-U function, where intermediate states yield optimal execution while hypo- or hyper-arousal leads to systemic performance degradation [@yerkes1908]. Adaptive Gain Theory provides a functional account of this classic relationship by frameworking arousal as a dynamic modulator of neural gain, which directly dictates the signal-to-noise ratio of information processing during task-relevant behavior [@astonjones2005]. When applied to the psychology of aging, empirical evidence suggests that the dynamic range of these autonomic regulation systems becomes significantly constricted. Age-related shifts in baseline arousal settings and diminished physiological flexibility make older adults highly vulnerable to over-activation. Consequently, modest increases in objective task demands can rapidly elevate systemic arousal past the optimal peak and into a supra-optimal zone where excessive internal noise compromises cognitive stability [@huang2024; @mather2016; @mikneviciute2022].

This physiological vulnerability becomes highly salient when cognitive operations are performed under concurrent physical load, which acts as a powerful somatic driver of systemic arousal. Because older adults exhibit reduced motor efficiency and diminished physiological reserves, maintaining an isometric grip demands a vastly disproportionate expenditure of subjective effort relative to younger cohorts. This cognitive-motor cost reflects an age-related shift wherein previously automated sensorimotor operations must recruit explicit, top-down executive control, effectively transforming a somatic task into a direct competitor for limited central processing resources [@verhaeghen2003]. Older adults performing continuous processing tasks exhibit exaggerated autonomic reactivity, measured via prominent shifts in systolic blood pressure, which directly predict heightened states of subsequent cognitive fatigue [@hess2012]. Crucially, this somatic burden directly interferes with simultaneous processing, selectively impairing performance accuracy in older adults under conditions where younger adults remain entirely unaffected [@azer2023]. Rather than treating resource competition [@wickens2008] and arousal-based models as independent accounts, we argue they are functionally integrated. The substantial central resources required to sustain a high-intensity physical grip force the aging nervous system into a state of hyper-arousal. This sustained somatic load pushes the organism past the optimal peak of the functional gain curve, generating a resource bottleneck where cognitive processing efficiency is simultaneously drained by structural capacity limits and obscured by hyper-arousal-induced noise.

Although it is clear that concurrent physical effort alters gross behavioral metrics like accuracy, traditional performance measures are fundamentally blind to the underlying latent mechanisms driving these failures. For example, a drop in accuracy under high physical load could reflect a degradation in the quality of sensory processing, but it could alternatively signal a top-down strategic shift where a participant deliberately lowers their decision threshold to escape the discomfort of sustained muscular contraction. Traditional reaction time and error analyses cannot adjudicate between these competing explanations. By decomposing behavioral data into distinct computational parameters within a diffusion framework, we can explicitly isolate these hidden components. Identifying whether physical effort selectively suppresses evidence quality or collapses decision boundaries provides critical insight into the functional architecture of cognitive-motor interference. This computational approach moves the field beyond merely documenting that physical demand impairs cognition, providing instead a clear mechanistic account of how somatic load shapes the speed, accuracy, and strategic boundaries of human choice.

## Pupillometry and Pupil-Informed Drift-Diffusion Modeling

To empirically capture these shifting states of resource allocation, we utilize pupillometry as a continuous physiological proxy for an individual's internal state. Non-invasive eye tracking provides a highly sensitive measure of central nervous system activation, where fluctuations in pupil diameter track changes in autonomic tone with exceptional temporal precision [@beatty1982; @kahneman1966]. Within this methodology, two distinct components offer insight into a participant's physiological state. While baseline pupil diameter reflects slower shifts in tonic arousal and sustained alertness, the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) acts as a rapid, phasic signal that directly tracks moment-to-moment changes in cognitive and somatic workload [@gilzenrat2010; @vangerven2004]. Quantifying this phasic response via the trial-wise area under the curve (AUC) allows us to measure how the immediate demand of sustaining a physical grip alters an individual's physiological investment from one choice to the next.

Of course, peripheral pupil metrics are not driven solely by internal arousal; they are inherently sensitive to extraneous variables such as ambient luminance, viewing distance, and direct motor execution reflexes [@beatty1982; @loewenfeld1999]. We rigorously control for these potential confounds by executing our paradigm within a highly regulated MRI environment characterized by constant background luminance and a locked viewing distance. Under these invariant conditions, transient changes in the TEPR can be confidently interpreted as a relative index of phasic arousal rather than a sensory or physical artifact. Furthermore, while a wealth of animal and neuropharmacological research firmly links transient pupil dilations to central locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity [@gilzenrat2010; @joshi2016], our psychophysiological approach treats the TEPR strictly as a functional, systemic index of phasic arousal state rather than a direct anatomical biomarker of midbrain nuclei integrity. However, an open physiological question remains whether the concurrent somatic demands of a sustained motor action complement or structurally obscure these transient, cognitively driven pupillary dilations under high workload.

Integrating this single-trial psychophysiological metric directly into a computational model offers a substantial analytical advantage over traditional behavioral modeling. Standard applications of the drift-diffusion model generate static parameter estimates averaged across entire blocks of trials. This aggregate approach completely ignores the reality that a participant's internal state fluctuations occur continuously throughout a session. By incorporating trial-by-trial pupil data directly into the hierarchical DDM framework, we can map these transient, phasic arousal fluctuations onto specific latent decision processes, revealing how moment-to-moment cognitive preparation shifts under the broader constraints of a sustained physical load.

A foundational demonstration of this technique was provided by Cavanagh and colleagues [-@cavanagh2014], who utilized single-trial pupillometry during a probabilistic learning task to show that transient pupil dilations specifically predicted an increase in boundary separation ($a$) during high-conflict choices. This finding suggested that under cognitive conflict, a sudden surge in phasic arousal acts as a signaling mechanism that prompts the brain to adopt greater response caution.

Our study extends this methodology by shifting the experimental focus from cognitive conflict to physical effort, and from healthy young cohorts to an aging population. This shift provides a fundamentally distinct test of how internal arousal states govern decision architecture. While cognitive conflict in young adults primarily modulates top-down strategic thresholds, the combination of advanced age and concurrent physical exertion introduces a severe strain on shared processing resources. Consequently, by testing pupil-informed models under varying physical loads—including nested extensions on drift, starting-point bias, and boundary separation—we evaluated whether trial-by-trial fluctuations in pupil-indexed phasic arousal track strategic caution ($a$) or degradation in evidence accumulation ($v$) under sustained physical load.

## Hypotheses and Predictions

We evaluated four primary predictions regarding how concurrent physical load modulates the latent components of decision formation in older adults. First, we hypothesized that the drift rate ($v$) would significantly decrease under the high-effort condition (40% MVC) relative to the low-effort baseline (5% MVC). This prediction directly builds upon the principles of resource competition and functional arousal dynamics established across the preceding sections. The severe somatic burden of maintaining a high-intensity muscular contraction is expected to force the aging nervous system past the optimal peak of the Yerkes-Dodson curve, draining shared central resources and ultimately degrading the clarity and efficiency of sensory evidence accumulation.

Second, we evaluated two competing accounts regarding boundary separation ($a$). Under an adaptive caution account extrapolated from cognitive conflict frameworks, systemic hyper-arousal might prompt a top-down, strategic widening of thresholds to protect performance stability under strain. Conversely, under a somatic fatigue account, the acute physical discomfort of sustained muscular contraction could drive a collapse of boundaries as participants attempt to terminate trials quickly. Adjudicating between these accounts allows us to determine whether older adults dynamically recalibrate their decision criteria under tonic somatic load.

Third, we addressed the impact of motor demand on peripheral overhead by exploring whether non-decision time ($t_0$) would increase under high physical effort, a shift that would reflect direct cognitive-motor interference during concurrent grip maintenance. Because the inherent structural constraints of the response-signal paradigm restrict full estimation flexibility for non-decision processes, this evaluation was treated as an explicit exploratory analysis rather than a primary structural hypothesis. These parameter variations are reported transparently to provide a complete overview of the model space despite these paradigm-specific mathematical limitations.

Fourth, we tested whether the bias-attenuating properties of physiological arousal generalize from transient states to sustained states. While spontaneous, trial-by-trial phasic arousal bursts have been shown to systematically suppress choice biases, it remains unknown whether a sustained, exogenously driven tonic elevation in arousal operates through an identical framework. We hypothesized that if tonic somatic noise mirrors phasic arousal dynamics, starting-point bias ($z$) would systematically shift toward structural neutrality ($z = 0.5$) under high effort; alternatively, the chronic overhead of the motor task might lock in stable, energy-saving strategic heuristics.

## The Present Study

The present chapter applies hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion modeling to examine how physical effort (Low: 5% MVC vs. High: 40% MVC isometric handgrip) modulates latent decision parameters in older adults performing auditory and visual same-different discrimination tasks. Trial-by-trial task-evoked pupil responses (TEPR) serve as an exploratory index of phasic arousal to test whether within-person arousal fluctuations predict changes in evidence accumulation or response bias. Together, these analyses test whether the characteristic slowing and cautiousness of older decision-makers reflect fixed capacity limits or physiological-state-dependent features modulated by effort-induced arousal.

# Methods

```{r ddm-sample-counts-early}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# Task participation after primary RT cutoff (shared by Methods + Results)
n_single_task_ddm <- NA_integer_
n_subj_adt_ddm <- NA_integer_
n_subj_vdt_ddm <- NA_integer_
.ddm_paths <- c(
  file.path(proj_root, "output", "rt_threshold_analysis", "ddm_ready_data.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data", "ddm_ready_data.csv")
)
for (.dp in .ddm_paths) {
  if (!file.exists(.dp)) next
  .td <- readr::read_csv(.dp, show_col_types = FALSE)
  .task_col <- intersect(c("task", "Task"), names(.td))[1]
  .subj_col <- intersect(c("subject_id", "sub"), names(.td))[1]
  .rt_col <- intersect(c("rt", "same_diff_resp_secs", "rt_cue_locked"), names(.td))[1]
  if (is.null(.task_col) || is.null(.subj_col)) next
  .td <- .td %>%
    dplyr::mutate(Task = dplyr::case_when(
      !!rlang::sym(.task_col) %in% c("ADT", "aud", "Auditory") ~ "ADT",
      !!rlang::sym(.task_col) %in% c("VDT", "vis", "Visual") ~ "VDT",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(Task))
  if (!is.null(.rt_col) && .rt_col %in% names(.td)) {
    .td <- .td %>%
      dplyr::filter(!is.na(!!rlang::sym(.rt_col)), !!rlang::sym(.rt_col) >= PRIMARY_THR)
  }
  .adt_subs <- unique(.td[[.subj_col]][.td$Task == "ADT"])
  .vdt_subs <- unique(.td[[.subj_col]][.td$Task == "VDT"])
  n_subj_adt_ddm <- length(.adt_subs)
  n_subj_vdt_ddm <- length(.vdt_subs)
  n_single_task_ddm <- length(setdiff(.adt_subs, .vdt_subs)) +
    length(setdiff(.vdt_subs, .adt_subs))
  break
}
```

## Participants

Participants were recruited from communities surrounding the University of California, Riverside, through multiple channels including direct mail, posted flyers, social media advertisements, and word-of-mouth referrals. Eligibility criteria required participants to be aged 60–90 years, possess normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, demonstrate sufficient English language comprehension to follow experimental instructions, and exhibit right-hand dominance. Exclusion criteria comprised contraindications for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), current use of psychotropic medications, clinically significant neurological disorders, and major systemic health conditions including diabetes mellitus. 

Sixty-nine individuals initially enrolled in the study. Two participants were excluded following enrollment: one due to suspected mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and another due to possible essential tremor, yielding a final sample of `r methods_n_sample` older adults (age *M* = `r methods_age_mean` years, *SD* = `r methods_age_sd`, range = `r methods_age_range` years). Table 1 reports baseline demographics for the full sample; the extended neuropsychological battery and additional baseline descriptives are provided in Appendix A9. After applying the RT threshold and quality criteria (fewer than 100 analyzable trials in a given task), `r if (exists("n_single_task_ddm") && !is.na(n_single_task_ddm)) n_single_task_ddm else "five"` participants contributed data to only one task, yielding task-specific analytic samples of *N* = `r if (exists("n_subj_adt_ddm")) n_subj_adt_ddm else 64` (Auditory) and *N* = `r if (exists("n_subj_vdt_ddm")) n_subj_vdt_ddm else 65` (Visual). Sample size was determined via a priori power analysis (G\*Power 3.1; [@faul2007g]). For a repeated-measures ANOVA with two within-subject conditions, medium effect size ($f = 0.25$), $\alpha = .05$, and power = .80, a minimum of 34 participants was required. The achieved sample of $N = 67$ exceeds this threshold by approximately 2$\times$ and is consistent with published hierarchical DDM studies reliably detecting group-level condition effects with $N = 30$–$60$ [@ratcliff2004aging; @wiecki2013hddm]. Twelve participants performed at or near chance level ($\leq$ 55% accuracy, compared to the 50% two-alternative forced-choice chance baseline) in some experimental conditions but were retained in analyses to maximize sample size, as hierarchical modeling approaches borrow statistical strength across participants to stabilize individual-level parameter estimates.

All participants provided written informed consent and received either course credit or monetary compensation for their participation. Study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, Riverside, and all experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with approved guidelines and regulations.

# Function to calculate demographics for a dataset
calc_demographics <- function(data) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  
  # Age
  age_mean <- mean(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_sd <- sd(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', age_mean, age_sd)
  
  # Gender
  female_count <- sum(data$sex == 'female', na.rm = TRUE)
  female_pct <- round(100 * female_count / n, 1)
  gender_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', female_count, female_pct)
  
  # Education
  edu_mean <- mean(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_sd <- sd(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', edu_mean, edu_sd)
  
  # MoCA
  if ('moca' %in% names(data)) {
    moca_mean <- mean(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_sd <- sd(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', moca_mean, moca_sd)
  } else {
    moca_str <- 'N/A'
  }
  
  # Race categorization
  race_clean <- data$race
  has_white <- grepl('white', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_black <- grepl('black|african', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_asian <- grepl('^asian$|^asian,', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white
  has_other <- grepl('other', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian
  
  race_cat <- rep(NA_character_, length(race_clean))
  race_cat[has_white] <- 'White/Caucasian'
  race_cat[has_black & !has_white] <- 'Black/African American'
  race_cat[has_asian & !has_white & !has_black] <- 'Asian'
  race_cat[has_other & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian] <- 'Other'
  race_cat[is.na(race_clean)] <- NA_character_
  
  white_count <- sum(race_cat == 'White/Caucasian', na.rm = TRUE)
  white_pct <- round(100 * white_count / n, 1)
  white_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', white_count, white_pct)
  
  black_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Black/African American', na.rm = TRUE)
  black_pct <- round(100 * black_count / n, 1)
  black_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', black_count, black_pct)
  
  asian_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Asian', na.rm = TRUE)
  asian_pct <- round(100 * asian_count / n, 1)
  asian_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', asian_count, asian_pct)
  
  other_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Other', na.rm = TRUE)
  other_pct <- round(100 * other_count / n, 1)
  other_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', other_count, other_pct)
  
  # Hispanic/Latino - fix: exclude "Not Hispanic or Latino"
  hispanic_count <- sum(
    grepl('hispanic|latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE) & 
    !grepl('not hispanic|not latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  hispanic_pct <- round(100 * hispanic_count / n, 1)
  hispanic_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', hispanic_count, hispanic_pct)
  
  return(list(
    n = n, age = age_str, gender = gender_str, edu = edu_str, moca = moca_str,
    white = white_str, black = black_str, asian = asian_str, other = other_str,
    hispanic = hispanic_str
  ))
}

full_stats <- calc_demographics(full_demo)

  )
)

## Stimuli and Task Design

**Task overview** Participants completed two response-signal same/different discrimination tasks—an Auditory Detection Task (ADT) and a Visual Detection Task (VDT)—each performed under concurrent hand-grip effort manipulation. In both tasks, a standard and probe stimulus were presented in succession, and participants judged whether the stimuli were the same or different using button presses, followed by a confidence rating.

**Trial structure.** Both tasks shared the same response-signal timeline (see @fig-ddm-process, Panel A). Each trial began with a jittered blank interval (1.5–4.5 s) displaying only a gray background. Participants were then shown a 3-second rectangular grip gauge with a marker positioned at either 5% or 40% from the bottom, indicating the target force level to be maintained using a hand-held dynamometer (left hand) at the corresponding percentage of their maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). MVC was determined during a brief calibration procedure prior to each task. Following the grip period, a 0.25-second blank screen and 0.5-second fixation dot preceded stimulus presentation.

**Auditory Detection Task (ADT).** The standard stimulus was a 0.1-second sinusoidal tone at 1000 Hz. After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second tone that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta frequency$ = 0) or positively offset by $\Delta frequency \in \{8, 16, 32, 64\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. For drift-diffusion model (DDM) analyses, the four non-zero offsets were collapsed into two difficulty bins: Hard = {8, 16} Hz and Easy = {32, 64} Hz, with Standard = 0 Hz.

**Visual Detection Task (VDT).** The standard stimulus was a centrally presented sinusoidal Gabor patch (spatial frequency 1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, diameter 4°, duration 0.1 s). After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second Gabor that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta contrast$ = 0) or showed a positive contrast increase of $\Delta contrast \in \{0.06, 0.12, 0.24, 0.48\}$, with all other parameters held constant. For DDM analyses, offsets were collapsed into Hard = {0.06, 0.12} and Easy = {0.24, 0.48}, with Standard = 0.

**Response collection.** Following stimulus offset, participants relaxed their grip and had a 3-second response window to indicate whether the two stimuli were the same or different using their right hand (index finger = "different"; middle finger = "same"). This was immediately followed by another 3-second window in which participants provided a confidence rating on a 4-point scale (1 = low confidence, 4 = high confidence).

**Trial counts and monitoring.** Each task comprised 150 trials distributed across five blocks of 30 trials each. Within each block, the five stimulus levels (Standard plus four offsets) were crossed with the two effort conditions (5% vs. 40% MVC) and presented in pseudorandom order with equal proportions (three repetitions per stimulus × effort combination). Hand-grip performance was monitored after each block, and participants received corrective feedback if they consistently failed to maintain the dynamometer at the designated force level (near the grip gauge marker) and/or for the correct duration (until offset of the probe stimulus).

## Equipment

The experimental task was programmed and executed on an Alienware laptop. Visual stimuli were presented via a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 480 Hz refresh rate, 1920×1080 resolution) and viewed through a head coil-mounted mirror (viewing distance $\approx$ 12 cm). Auditory stimuli were delivered via MRI-safe earbuds (Newmatic Medical, Duluth, GA; 30 dB NRR). Behavioral responses were recorded using a RESPONSEpixx fiber-optic response box, hand-grip force via a MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs Inc., Philadelphia, USA; 100 Hz sampling), and pupil diameter via an MRI-compatible TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 2000 Hz sampling). Stimuli were generated using Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA). Data were collected inside an MRI scanner; neuroimaging results are reported elsewhere.

## Data Processing and Quality Control

**Reaction time definition.** In this response-signal design, reaction time (RT) was initially recorded as the latency from response-screen onset (“Same or Different?” prompt) to button press, termed **cue-locked RT**. However, perceptual evidence becomes available at probe onset (the second stimulus). To align RT with evidence accumulation onset, we derived **probe-onset-locked RT** by adding the fixed post-probe delay to cue-locked RT:

$$RT_{\text{probe-onset}} = RT_{\text{cue-locked}} + 0.35\text{ s}.$$ {#eq-probe}

where 0.35 s comprises 0.10 s probe duration plus 0.25 s grip-relaxation period. Probe-onset-locked RT served as the primary timing measure for DDM interpretation, as it aligns the decision process with evidence onset. Under this convention, the DDM non-decision time parameter ($t_0$) includes the fixed 0.35 s response-gating delay plus residual encoding and motor components. Cue-locked RT was retained for sensitivity analyses. This probe-onset-locked timing is our chosen convention to align $t_0$ with evidence onset; some DDM studies alternatively use cue-locked or response-locked reference points depending on task structure.

**Gated response-signal validity.** Overt responses were withheld until the response screen (a fixed 0.35 s after probe offset), so cue-locked RT mixes pre-response processing with enforced waiting. Probe-onset locking shifts the accumulation clock to evidence onset while absorbing the fixed gating interval into $t_0$ (intercept-only in the primary model). This follows standard practice for response-signal and masked-response designs: condition contrasts are identified within a shared timing regime, and absolute $t_0$ estimates are not interpreted as pure motor time [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @starns2010]. We treat probe-onset locking as a conservative alignment choice; free-response replications without enforced waiting would be needed to isolate encoding-only $t_0$ components.

**Trial exclusion criteria.** To minimize the influence of premature or accidental button presses, trials with cue-locked RT < 0.20 s were excluded from the primary analysis (sensitivity analyses using alternative cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s are reported in Appendix A). This lower bound was applied to cue-locked RT before constructing probe-onset-locked RT for the primary DDM models. Additional exclusions included missed responses, trials from runs flagged for invalid performance (defined as run-level accuracy at or below chance, indicating the participant did not engage with the task), and trials with non-positive or missing RT values (i.e., recording artifacts where RT was logged as zero or a negative number). For pupil-linked DDM models, trials additionally required valid pupil data (see Pupillometry Preprocessing section).
